Same reasoning as other effect-measure mislabels in this review: changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results; minor because the methods define the OR, J possible because the header invites extraction as an additive difference.

rows.R: Protocol defines the primary outcome as the proportion with '>1 SAE' (repeatedly) and results eTable 2 says 'Infant had > 1 SAE'; the main article and SAP say '≥1'/'at least 1'/'any'. Same counts (44/159, 27/149) appear under both labels. The SAP uses '>1' and 'at least one' in the same hypothesis passage, so '>1' is most likely a lost ≥ glyph.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.6 Table 2 ('Had ≥1 serious adverse event'); results supplement (supp3) eTable 2 (text, '> 1 SAE'); protocol (supp1) PDF p.2-3 and p.11; SAP (supp2) PDF p.2-4 (text).

Identical counts in Table 2 and eTable 2 show one analysis. Kept AI domain protocol_report; L=minor_presentation because the intended endpoint (any SAE) is clear from context, though the protocol's literal wording is wrong. The main-vs-eTable label mismatch is the same notational issue.

rows.R: Protocol p.3 hypothesizes median hospital days 18 (early) vs 15 (late); protocol p.12 power text assumes median 8/mean 18 vs median 5/mean 13. The SAP explicitly flags the p.3 values as incorrect and adopts 8 vs 5. Real but disclosed planning inconsistency; the 3-day hypothesized difference is unchanged.

Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: SAP: categorical-outcome intervention prior OR 95% CrI 0.2-4, Normal(0, SD 0.7) on log-OR; count outcomes RR 0.33-3.3. Article: one prior for categorical and count outcomes with 95% CrI 0.33-3.0 (implies SD about 0.56). For the primary (binary) outcome, the reported prior is tighter than planned; no amendment is supplied.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.4 Statistical Analysis (text); SAP (supp2) PDF p.8 (text).
rows.rationale: Quoted both. Computed: Normal(0, 0.7) gives exp(±1.96 x 0.7) = 0.25 to 3.94 (the SAP's approximate '0.2-4'); a 0.33-3.0 interval implies SD = ln(3)/1.96 = 0.56. The primary outcome is categorical, so the reported prior differs from the planned prior for the primary Bayesian analysis. The difference is modest in strength but is a change in analysis specification for a trial whose main result is a posterior probability. The SAP also specifies weakly informative priors for GA group (SD 1) and random-effect SD that the article summarizes as 'vague'. Kept AI domain; L=substantive_difference as a description of a planned-vs-reported analysis difference, not a judgment that results changed.

rows.R: Figure 3 and Methods use GA <28 wk vs ≥28 wk; SAP randomization strata and moderator text say '<28 weeks and >28 weeks', while the SAP covariate text says '≥ 28'. The two-group partition (<28 vs the rest) is clear; '>28' omits the boundary and reads as a notational slip.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.4 (text) and p.8 Figure 3 (text; 102+57=159, 99+50=149); SAP (supp2) PDF p.3, p.8, p.9 (text).
rows.rationale: Confirmed wording in each location. Figure 3 subgroup sizes partition the analysis populations (102+57=159; 99+50=149), so every infant was assigned and the upper group is the complement of <28. The SAP is itself inconsistent (> vs ≥). Minor wording difference; intended boundary clear. Kept AI domain.

rows.R: All documents use enrollment and randomization interchangeably as time zero: the protocol says both '10 months after randomization' and '10 months after enrollment', the SAP says both, and the main article says data were collected '10 months after randomization' and families contacted '10 months after enrollment'. Randomization occurred at consent/enrollment.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.3 (randomization at consent via REDCap; '10 months after randomization'), p.4 ('10 months after enrollment'), p.6 Table 2 footnote g; protocol (supp1) PDF p.3, p.11 and consent section (randomized when consent obtained); SAP (supp2) PDF p.2 and p.4 (text).
rows.rationale: Text search found both terms in each document, including within the protocol (p.3 '10 months after randomization' alongside '10 months after enrollment'). The main Methods state that once eligibility and consent were confirmed, REDCap assigned an ID and randomized the infant, so enrollment and randomization coincide operationally. No planned-versus-reported difference; the AI statement that the main article uses only randomization is not accurate. Exclude.

rows.R: Article says GI-3 at '72 hours after surgery/operation'; SAP and protocol define '72 hours after the start of operation'. The planning documents themselves use 'after surgery' as shorthand (e.g., PPOI 'by 120 hours after surgery' in both protocol and SAP, defined elsewhere from start of operation). No evidence of a different time zero.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1, p.4 Outcomes, p.6 Table 2 (rendered); SAP (supp2) PDF p.9 (text); protocol (supp1) PDF p.16-17 (text).

The protocol's own endpoint list gives 'Prolonged Postoperative Ileus (failure to establish GI-3 by 120 hours after surgery)' immediately above 'Specific time-point: 120 hours after start of operation', and the SAP repeats '120 hours after surgery'. The article's Table 2 footnotes use 'start of operation' for other timed items. 'After surgery' is therefore the trial's shorthand for the defined origin, and counts match across documents. Compatible statements, so exclude (codebook: non_inconsistency normally means exclude). Disagree with the AI retain suggestion.

rows.R: Protocol: total postoperative opioid consumption as cumulative morphine equivalents until 72 hours after start of operation; SAP: total in-hospital opioid consumption up to 72 hours. Article lists and reports postoperative opioid consumption up to 24 hours (median OME 70.6 vs 45.0 mg, n=210 each). No amendment or explanation is given.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.4 Outcomes (text), p.5 Results text, p.6 Table 2 (rendered); protocol (supp1) PDF p.17 (text); SAP (supp2) PDF p.11 (text).
rows.rationale: Verified the 72-hour definitions in protocol and SAP and the 24-hour definition and results in the article. The only amendment the article mentions concerns consent during COVID-19. A 24-hour cumulative dose is a different measurement window from 72 hours and cannot be converted. Secondary outcome, but a real planned-versus-reported difference in an outcome definition. Kept AI domain; L=substantive_difference.

rows.R: Article Methods define the tertiary outcome as 'unplanned readmission within 30 days of surgery' (as do the protocol and SAP, including the SAP table shell), but Table 3 reports 'Unplanned readmission after discharge and within 90 d of operation' 31 (11.1) vs 34 (12.2). Hospital records were checked at days 30 and 90, so either window is possible.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.4 Outcomes and Follow-up (text), p.8 Table 3 (text); protocol (supp1) PDF p.18; SAP (supp2) PDF p.10 and Table 13.23 shell (text).
rows.rationale: Confirmed: 31/279=11.1% and 34/278=12.2% (Python) reproduce the printed percentages but not the window. The article itself conflicts (Methods 30 days vs Table 3 90 days), and the article states readmission data were collected from records at days 30 and 90, so the reader cannot tell which window the counts represent. 30- and 90-day readmission are distinct outcomes, so the inconsistency changes how the result is understood. Changed E from protocol_report to report_internal_inconsistency because the decisive conflict is within the main article; if the counts are 90-day counts, there is also an unexplained planned-vs-reported change.

rows.R: Protocol gives ERAS compliance bands only as an example ('e.g. 0-30%, 30-60%, >60%'); the SAP names high/moderate/low without cut points; the eFigure footnote states the subgroup was preplanned but the category definitions were not predefined, and gives them (high >=7/10, low <5/10). Disclosed; no fixed plan was contradicted.
rows.evidence: protocol (supp1) PDF p.18 (ERAS compliance metric 'e.g.' bands, text) and p.41; SAP (supp2) PDF p.14-15; results supplement (supp3) PDF p.2 eFigure and footnote (rendered).
rows.rationale: Read all three sources. The protocol bands are explicitly illustrative, the SAP leaves cut points unspecified, and the report discloses that its cut points were defined post hoc. On a 10-item score the protocol example and the report differ only at 4/10 (40%). Because no binding planned definition existed and the report is transparent, this is not a meaningful planned-versus-reported discrepancy; exclude. Disagree with the AI retain suggestion.

rows.R: eFigure legend labels the subgroup interval lines '99% CI'; the caption says the right-hand numbers are '95% confidence interval'. The plotted lines match the printed numbers (e.g., low adherence 0.49-2.08), and the overall row 0.97 (0.88, 1.07) equals the main-text 95% CI. The SAP planned 99% CIs for subgroups. Interval level is ambiguous.
rows.evidence: results supplement (supp3) PDF p.2 eFigure (rendered, axis positions compared with printed limits); main PDF p.6 Table 2; SAP (supp2) PDF p.15 (text).
rows.rationale: Confirmed the conflicting labels. I compared bar endpoints with the axis (0.5 to 2 scale) for the overall and low-adherence rows; the bars coincide with the printed limits, so lines and numbers are the same intervals. The overall row matches the 95% CI in Table 2, which suggests 95% throughout and contradicts the legend and the SAP's 99% plan, but I cannot verify the subgroup interval level without data. Confirmed labeling conflict; minor because all intervals include 1 and interaction P values are reported; J possible for anyone extracting subgroup CIs.

rows.R: Results state there was no significant difference in quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), but Table 2 gives day 5 difference -0.057 (95% CI -0.111 to -0.003), P=.04 (favoring placebo; n=89 vs 96). One of 9 unadjusted time points; the blanket statement is literally inaccurate though the overall pattern is null.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.5 Results text and p.6 Table 2 EQ-5D rows (rendered); SAP (supp2) PDF p.13-14 (no multiplicity adjustment for secondary outcomes, text).
rows.rationale: Verified the table row and the prose. The CI excludes 0 and P=.04, so the sentence 'no significant difference in ... quality of life' does not hold for day 5 under the paper's own nominal 95% framework. Given 9 time points without adjustment, a single nominal result is weak evidence, and the summary may intend the outcome overall; hence probable rather than confirmed, and minor because it does not change the trial's conclusions. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Article Methods list the preplanned subgroup as 'high vs low enhanced recovery protocol adherence', but the eFigure (and SAP) analyze three levels: high n=191, moderate n=274, low n=92 (sum 557), with one interaction P=.966. Two-level wording is shorthand for the three-level factor actually analyzed.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.4 Outcomes/subgroups and p.5 Results (text); results supplement (supp3) PDF p.2 eFigure (rendered); SAP (supp2) PDF p.14-15 (text).

Changed E from protocol_report to report_internal_inconsistency because the reported analysis agrees with the plan and the discrepancy lies between the main article and its supplement. Minor.

rows.R: eTable 2 liberal walk-in transport 4/743 (5.3); 4/743 = 0.5%. The liberal transport counts sum to 743 (585+141+9+3+4+1) and the other percentages are correct, so the count is right and 5.3 is a misplaced-decimal error (column percentages sum to 104.7%).

Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: The further-adjusted primary-outcome OR for all patients is 0.98 (0.68 to 1.41) in eTable 4 but 0.98 (0.68 to 1.39) in eTable 7, with identical counts. The article describes a single additional adjusted model, so the intervals should match; the 0.02 difference does not affect interpretation.

Changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results because the question is the reported CI of an estimate. Minor.

rows.R: AIS <3 subgroup, liberal arm: Figure 4 prints 48/473 (10.1) and eTable 7 prints 48/473 (9.2). 48/473 = 10.1%, so eTable 7 is wrong; 9.2 matches the liberal value in the row above (50/543), suggesting a copy error.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.8 Figure 4 (rendered); supp2 PDF p.20 eTable 7 (rendered).

Changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results because it is a count/percentage arithmetic error.

rows.R: Known lung disease, liberal arm: Figure 4 14/69 (20.3) vs eTable 7 14/69 (20.2). 14/69 = 20.29%, so 20.3 is correct. eTable 7 otherwise rounds (e.g., 68/238 -> 28.6, 70/430 -> 16.3), so truncation does not explain it. 0.1-point error.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.8 Figure 4 (rendered); supp2 PDF p.20 eTable 7 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Recomputed every eTable 7 percentage with counts: cells where rounding and truncation differ (68/238, 70/430, 67/428) are rounded, so the table convention is rounding. Confirmed; trivial. Changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results for consistency with other arithmetic findings.

rows.R: eTable 10 row 'Exclusion after randomization (N=130)' prints 55 and 67 (sum 122), and its percentages 45/55 are shares of 122. Figure 1 gives 59 and 71 (sum 130). Each arm differs by 4, matching the 4 per arm 'omitted according to Swiss law due to withdrawn consent', but eTable 10 does not say so.

The likely explanation (no oxygen data for the 8 Swiss-law omissions) is plausible but unstated, and the row label N=130 is wrong for the printed counts. Confirmed. Minor: a descriptive supplementary table on excluded patients, not an analysis population. Changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results because the issue is a count/total mismatch.

rows.R: eTable 10 secondary exclusions printed as 174/750 (51) and 165/758 (49): 174/750 = 23.2% and 165/758 = 21.8%, while 51%/49% are shares of the 339 classified exclusions. Also, 750/758 are the analyzed patients who received oxygen, of whom excluded patients are not a subset. Counts match Figure 1.
rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.24 eTable 10 (rendered); main PDF p.3 Figure 1 (rendered).

Figure 1 shows 983-59-174=750 and 994-71-165=758, so the excluded patients lie outside the 750/758 denominators printed in the cells. Confirmed denominator misuse in the display; minor because counts are correct and the table is descriptive. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: eTable 11 prints the restrictive missing-as-event primary count as '135//750 (18.0)' with a doubled slash. 135/750 = 18.0% reconciles; typographic defect only.
rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.25 eTable 11 (rendered).

rows.R: Abstract phase-2 allocations mix denominators: CNRT 90 (47%) = 90/191 but 50 (33%) and 51 (34%) = /151; varenicline 39 (32%) and 41 (34%) = /122 but 77 (49%) = /157. Percentages sum to 114% and 115%. Counts are correct (90+50+51 = 191; 39+41+77 = 157).

rows.rationale: Recomputed in Python: 90/191=47.1%, 50/191=26.2%, 51/191=26.7%, 50/151=33.1%, 51/151=33.8%; 39/122=32.0%, 41/122=33.6%, 77/157=49.0%. The continuation groups include the 40 and 35 nonattenders, so the 'continued' percentages use all nonabstainers while the others use only those rerandomized. Confirmed; minor because the counts are right. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Main Table: each arm (n = 245) shows female 105 (42.9) and male 145 (57.1); 105 + 145 = 250. 57.1% of 245 is 140, and eTable 3 phase-2 subgroups sum to 140 males per arm (CNRT 33+30+49+28; varenicline 50+19+44+27). Male count should be 140.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.5 Table (text); supp2 PDF p.19 eTable 3 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Recomputed: 140/245=57.1%, 145/245=59.2%; abstract 210 women (43%) = 105+105 of 490. eTable 3 female sums 105 and male sums 140 in both arms. Confirmed transcription error in the male count; percentages and female counts are right, so minor.

rows.R: Figure 2 shows 491 randomized but branches of 245 + 245 = 490; the CNRT box says 245 randomized, 245 received treatment, 1 did not (footnote b: assigned to wrong phase-2 condition, excluded from all analyses), i.e., 246. Results text explains one CNRT participant was eliminated after randomization; the abstract says 490 were randomized.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.4 Results (text), p.6 Figure 2 and footnote b (rendered).
rows.rationale: 491-490=1, and 245+1=246 within the CNRT box. The text discloses the exclusion, so the figure's arm count of 245 'randomized to CNRT' and the abstract's '490 volunteers were randomized' are inaccurate rather than unexplained. Confirmed; minor. Note for interpretation: excluding a randomized participant from all analyses departs from strict intention to treat, which the paper discloses.

rows.R: Results: 'the 40 participants in the phase 1 CNRT group and the 35 in the varenicline group who did attend rerandomization were assigned to continue'. Abstract and Figure 2: these 40 and 35 did not return/attend and were assigned (imputed) to continuation. A missing 'not'; the counts match.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.4 Results (text), p.6 Figure 2 boxes and footnote c (rendered).
rows.rationale: Confirmed the contradictory wording. Changed E from statistical_results to report_internal_inconsistency because the conflict is in a narrative description, not a number. Rated minor because the abstract and figure state the correct status. Separately (not the candidate), placing non-rerandomized nonattenders into the continuation arm (40/90 CNRT, 35/77 varenicline) means the continuation comparator is partly nonrandomized, which matters for interpreting the phase-2 contrasts.

rows.R: Abstract gives 'RD, 6%; 95% CrI, 6% to 11%' after listing both CNRT rescue arms; Results say both increase and switch had RD 6% (95% CrI 2%-11%), and eTable 4 gives increase vs stay 6% (2%, 11%). A CrI whose lower limit equals the estimate is implausible; for the increased-dose contrast the abstract interval is wrong if the parenthetical covers it.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.5 Results (text); supp2 PDF p.21 eTable 4 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Results and eTable 4 agree on 2%-11% for increase vs continuation. The abstract parenthetical is attached grammatically to the switch arm but followed by 'either strategy', so its application to the increase contrast is likely but not certain; hence probable. Substantive because it misstates the uncertainty of a primary-outcome contrast in the abstract (lower limit 6% vs 2%), and J=direct because abstract values are commonly extracted. See C006 for the switch contrast.

rows.R: CNRT switch-to-varenicline vs continuation, primary outcome: abstract RD 6% (95% CrI 6%-11%); Results 6% (2%-11%); eTable 4 6% (2%, 10%). The abstract lower limit equals the point estimate and conflicts with both other sources; Results and eTable also differ in the upper limit.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.5 Results (text); supp2 PDF p.21 eTable 4 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Read all three. Three different intervals for one primary-outcome contrast; the abstract's 6%-11% is implausible and substantially overstates precision relative to 2%-11%/2%-10%. Confirmed. Substantive because it concerns the abstract's primary-outcome estimate for a recommended rescue strategy; the 10% vs 11% upper-limit difference alone would be minor. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Varenicline nonabstainers: switch to CNRT 0% (0/41) vs continuation 3% (2/77). Results give RD -3% (-4% to -1%) yet say there was >99% probability 'that continuing was worse than switching'; eTable 4 labels the contrast switch vs stay but prints +3% (1%, 4%). The data show switching was worse; the narrative and eTable sign are reversed.
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 abstract, p.5 Results (text); supp2 PDF p.21 eTable 4 (rendered).
rows.rationale: 0%-3% = -3 points (switch minus continuation), matching the Results RD; the accompanying sentence inverts the direction, the eTable sign contradicts its own 'switch vs stay' label, and the abstract's version ('continuing ... was worse than switching to a higher dosage') is garbled. Confirmed. Substantive because the stated direction of a phase-2 comparison is reversed in the main Results, which could lead a reader to favor switching. Changed E from report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results because the issue is the sign and interpretation of an estimate.

rows.R: Increased varenicline vs continuation, primary outcome: abstract and Results give RD 18% (95% CrI 13%-24%); eTable 4 gives 18% (13%, 23%). One-point difference in the upper limit; point estimate consistent with 8/39 vs 2/77 (20.5% - 2.6% = 17.9 points).
rows.evidence: main PDF p.1 and p.5 (text); supp2 PDF p.21 eTable 4 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Confirmed the mismatch. Likely a rounding or transcription difference between outputs; it does not change interpretation. Minor. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Phase-1 abstainers, CNRT vs varenicline at week 12: Results give RD 6% (95% CrI -5% to 16%); eTable 4 gives 6% (-4%, 16%). One-point difference in the lower limit (cells 42/54 = 78% vs 63/88 = 72%).
rows.evidence: main PDF p.7 Results (text); supp2 PDF p.21 eTable 4 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Confirmed. 42/54=77.8% and 63/88=71.6% (Python) support RD of about 6 points. Small interval discrepancy for a non-primary contrast; minor. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Protocol Figure 2 labels varenicline week-6 response '0.50, 0.40-0.60 ~Beta(785, 869)', but Beta(785, 869) has mean 0.475 and 95% interval 0.451-0.499. The NRT response Beta(193, 210) also gives 0.430-0.528, not 0.38-0.58. All eight phase-2 outcome Betas reproduce their printed summaries. Simulation-input documentation error.
rows.evidence: protocol (supp1) PDF p.32 Figure 2 (rendered); p.33 Table 2 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Computed Beta means and 2.5/97.5% quantiles with scipy for all ten distributions. Phase-2 Betas match their labels (e.g., Beta(62.2, 21.0): 0.748, 0.650-0.834 vs 0.75, 0.65-0.83), but both phase-1 response Betas are far too concentrated for their stated intervals, and the varenicline one also has the wrong mean. Real within-protocol inconsistency in power-simulation inputs; minor because it affects documentation of assumptions rather than the trial's analyses or results. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Protocol Table 3, Aim 1: power to detect posterior probability >0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95 is 0.948, 0.980, 0.974, 0.963. Power cannot increase as the threshold tightens on the same simulations; every other block in the table is monotone. With K = 1,000 runs (Monte Carlo SE about 0.007), a 0.032 rise is implausible as noise.
rows.evidence: protocol (supp1) PDF p.32 text (K = 1,000 simulations) and p.34 Table 3 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Checked monotonicity across all blocks: Aims 2-5 decrease with the threshold; only Aim 1 rises from 0.80 to 0.85. MC SE = sqrt(0.95 x 0.05 / 1000) = 0.0069. Most likely a transcription error in one cell. Minor: all values exceed the 80% power claim. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Protocol Table 3 Aim 2 lists 'VAR vs. NPL' twice (0.370 and 0.195). From Table 2 cell estimates: VAR - NPL = 0.399 - 0.029 = 0.370; NPL+ - NPL = 0.175; VAR - NPL+ = 0.399 - 0.204 = 0.195. The third row should be 'VAR vs. NPL+', as specified in the Aim 2 contrasts.

rows.R: eTable 3 (n (%) heading) race 'Other' for varenicline nonabstainers switched to CNRT (N = 41) prints '4.9 (2)'; 2/41 = 4.9%, so count and percentage are reversed. Values are correct and recoverable.
rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.19 eTable 3 (rendered).

rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.10 narrative (text); supp2 PDF p.15 eFigure 2 (rendered).

Correct values are in eFigure 2, and these are descriptive secondary outcomes without multiplicity correction, so minor. Agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Narrative EOT+30 probability for CNRT nonabstainers with increased dose: '8.0% (5.0%-1.1%)'; eFigure 2: 4/50, 8% (5%-11%). Upper limit misformatted (11 -> 1.1).
rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.10 (text); supp2 PDF p.15 eFigure 2 (rendered).

rows.R: Narrative EOT+30 ARD for CNRT switch vs continuation: '6.0% (3.0%-1.0%)'; eTable 9: 6% (3%-10%). Upper limit misformatted (10 -> 1.0); as printed the interval excludes the estimate.
rows.evidence: supp2 PDF p.10 (text); supp2 PDF p.33 eTable 9 (rendered).
